intro.title: Encrypted against an adversary from the day after tomorrow

adversary.title: Almost every messenger encrypts. The difference lies in what against.
paragraphs: Methods common today rest on mathematical problems a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve. Nobody knows when such machines will exist — that intercepted data is kept until they do is, by contrast, common practice.
Silvra therefore combines classical cryptography with ML-KEM, the method standardised in 2024 by the US standards institute NIST. Both together, not one alone: if one breaks, the other still holds.
adversary.highlight: The keys live exclusively on your devices. We cannot read your messages — not even on official request, because there is simply nothing readable there.
adversary.resultNote: If one breaks, the other holds.
adversary.diagramAlt: Diagram: X25519 and ML-KEM-768 combine into the hybrid X-Wing key that carries the MLS encryption. If one scheme breaks, the other still protects it.

helix.subtitle: A layer-1 blockchain secured by NIST-standardised post-quantum cryptography — every signature ML-DSA-65, from the very first block.

live.title: The chain, block by block.
live.lead: Every new block shows up here as soon as the public node reports it — with its height, hash and transactions. A click opens it in the explorer.

intro.title: Not retrofitted. Built from the ground up.
intro.body: Instead of migrating an existing chain to post-quantum later, Helix is designed for it from the first line of code: ML-DSA-65 on every transaction, block, and validator vote — no transition period, no classical curves to swap out down the line.

why.title: What existing chains leave open.
why.lead: Six problems Helix does not plan to solve some day, but from the first line of code.

rows.problem: ECDSA and Ed25519 signatures fall to a large quantum computer
rows.helix: ML-DSA-65 (NIST FIPS 204) on every transaction, block and vote

rows.problem: Stake buys voting power without limit
rows.helix: At most 1% of the vote per validator — however much capital is behind it

rows.problem: Hex addresses, and a lost key is final
rows.helix: alice.hlx names and recovery through guardians

rows.problem: No plan for the next cryptographic migration
rows.helix: The signature scheme is versioned in every transaction

rows.problem: Zero-knowledge proofs resting on elliptic curves (SNARKs)
A contract that runs forever stalls the chain
rows.helix: WASM VM, fuel-metered per transaction and per block, no floating point

chain.title: Eight decisions, block by block
chain.lead: What the protocol is made of — and where to read it in the code.

features.title: ML-DSA-65 everywhere
features.body: Every transaction, every block, every validator vote. No classical scheme with a migration plan attached.

features.title: Crypto agility built in
features.body: The signature scheme is versioned in every transaction; SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) stands by as a hash-based reserve.

features.title: Final in about two seconds
features.body: Tendermint-style BFT consensus: a block stands once two thirds of the vote is behind it — and is never reverted.

features.title: A 1% cap on voting power
features.body: No validator holds more than one percent of the vote. Capital does not automatically mean control.

features.title: Names and recovery
features.body: alice.hlx instead of a hex address — and social recovery through guardians when a key is lost.

features.title: WASM contracts without reentrancy
features.body: Fuel-metered, no floating point, no calls between contracts: the best-known attack surface simply is not there.

features.title: ZK-STARKs
features.body: Zero-knowledge proofs built on hashes alone — no elliptic curves for a quantum computer to break.

features.title: Upgrades by governance
features.body: Protocol changes are voted on-chain and activate at a height announced in advance. No more resets since 1.0.0.

supply.title: Scarce, traceable, no pre-mine.
supply.lead: Every number is in the code. More than 99% of all HLX only come into being by producing blocks.
supply.chartTitle: HLX supply over time — the ceiling, before burns
supply.aria: Line chart: HLX supply rises from 100,000 at genesis to about 31.6 million after 30 years, as the block reward halves every year. The hard cap is 33 million. Use the arrow keys to pick a year.

honesty.title: A young network — and we say so.

items.title: The validator set is still small
items.body: n validators survive ⌊(n−1)/3⌋ failures: four survive one, seven survive two. When too many are missing the chain stops and waits — it does not fork. The current number is shown above, live.

items.title: HLX is not an investment
items.body: Since 1.0.0 nothing is reset any more. That does not mean HLX is worth anything — and we don't claim it is.

items.title: The transport uses classical encryption
items.body: Nodes connect over libp2p Noise (X25519). What they exchange is public and ML-DSA-signed: a quantum computer could read along but forge nothing.

items.title: Consensus at scale: tested, not yet proven
items.body: Vote locking, re-proposals and double-signing go through chaos tests with a third of all messages lost — with no fork. The live network is still small.

items.title: Reviewed continuously from an attacker's side
items.body: Every finding is reproduced as a test before it is fixed — and each fix is checked by reverting it and watching the test fail again.

honesty.highlight: We'd rather say this upfront than have to explain it afterwards.

items.q: Do I need my own node?
items.a: No. The wallet and the command line talk to the public network with no setup. A node of your own is worth it if you want to validate or verify the chain independently.

items.q: How do I become a validator?
items.a: With at least 10,000 HLX staked and a running node — from the command line or at a click in the desktop wallet, behind NAT or a proxy too. The guide is in the documentation under “Running a Node”.

items.q: Can I take part without running a node?
items.a: Yes, by delegating: you put your stake behind a validator and receive a share of its earnings, less commission (10% by default, at most 50%).

items.q: What happens when validators go down?
items.a: With n validators the network survives ⌊(n−1)/3⌋ failures. With more missing, the chain stops and waits — it does not fork. A validator that stops signing is suspended for a while, but not penalised for it.
A base fee per byte, burned in full, plus a tip for the validator. The base fee follows demand (at most ±12.5% per block); the wallet never pays more than 1 HLX on its own.
No. The network is young, and nothing here promises it is worth anything.

mission.title: What is intercepted today can be read later
mission.subtitle: We build digital infrastructure that can still be accounted for even with quantum computers — and that originates in Europe.

approach.statement: Post-quantum cryptography from the start — built in while a project is young enough to take it without a break.
paragraphs: Much of the encryption carrying the internet today relies on mathematical problems that a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve. No one knows when such computers will exist. What is certain: anything intercepted and stored today can be decrypted later.
That is why, wherever we have the choice, we rely from the start on the methods standardized by NIST in 2024 — and build them in while a project is still young enough to do so without breaking.
The second motive is simpler: we want European alternatives to exist. Not as a label, but as software people can actually use.

accessibility.title: Accessibility statement
accessibility.subtitle: This site should work for everyone — by keyboard, with a screen reader, magnified or without any animation at all.

sections.title: Aim
sections.body: We build silvra.net to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2, conformance level AA. This statement covers silvra.net and all its pages; the Helix explorer and outside services such as Google Play or GitHub are not part of it.

sections.title: Compliance status
sections.body: By our checks, silvra.net is largely compliant with WCAG 2.2 AA. The known limitations are listed below.

sections.title: What the site does for it
items: A switch “Pause motion and live values” in the header stops every animation and every self-updating number; the operating system's “reduce motion” setting is honoured as well.
Everything can be reached by keyboard, focus is always visible, and a “skip to content” link opens every page. On the home page, ← and → choose a sector.
Text reaches a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 : 1, in the light and the dark theme.
Status is never conveyed by colour alone, always with a symbol and a word as well.
Every page is delivered as finished HTML and readable without JavaScript; headings, landmarks and language are marked up.
The site can be zoomed to 400 % and used down to 320 pixels wide without scrolling sideways.

sections.title: How we check
sections.body: Before every release we test each page in the light and the dark theme with axe-core against WCAG 2.2 A and AA, measure contrast and touch targets, and test keyboard operation. Last check: 7 October 2026.

sections.title: Known limitations
sections.body: What we are still working on:
items: There is currently no content in Easy Read or in sign language.
The encrypted-looking characters behind the home page are decoration and hidden from screen readers; what they show is said in the text.
The Helix explorer is a separate application with a very dense display; it is not covered by this statement.
